variants.title: Budget the miss path
variants.context: The hit rate is an outcome, not a capacity plan. Edge misses = viewer requests × (1 − hit rate), and every miss reaches the origin unless a centralized layer consolidates duplicates.
variants.prompt: A launch drives 100,000 viewer requests per second at a 95% edge hit rate. How many requests per second reach the origin?
variants.hint: Multiply viewer requests by the miss rate.
variants.explanation: 100,000 × 0.05 = 5,000 origin requests per second. The origin must be load-tested for that, not for the average.

mistakes.feedback: That is the hit count; misses are what reach the origin.

variants.title: Budget the miss path
variants.context: The hit rate is an outcome, not a capacity plan. Edge misses = viewer requests × (1 − hit rate), and every miss reaches the origin unless a centralized layer consolidates duplicates.
variants.prompt: Viewer traffic is 40,000 requests per second with a 92% hit rate. How many requests per second reach the origin?
variants.explanation: 40,000 × 0.08 = 3,200 requests per second. Cold objects and invalidations push this higher.

mistakes.feedback: That is the number of hits.

variants.title: Budget the miss path
variants.context: The hit rate is an outcome, not a capacity plan. Edge misses = viewer requests × (1 − hit rate), and every miss reaches the origin unless a centralized layer consolidates duplicates.
variants.prompt: The origin is load-tested to 2,500 requests per second. Viewer traffic peaks at 50,000 per second. What minimum edge hit rate, in percent, keeps the origin inside its tested capacity?
variants.hint: Misses must stay at or below origin capacity.
variants.explanation: 2,500 ÷ 50,000 = 5% misses, so the hit rate must be at least 95%. Origin Shield can consolidate duplicate misses for extra margin.

mistakes.feedback: 5% is the maximum miss rate; the hit rate is the complement.
90% would send 5,000 per second, double the tested capacity.

variants.title: Design the cache key
variants.context: Two requests may share a cached response only when every input that can change the response is in the cache key or removed by safe normalization. Name the response, list its inputs, normalize noise, then test isolation.
variants.prompt: A product page is being cached. Put the cache-key design steps in order.

items.text: Name the response with a stable, versioned object path.
List every query, header, cookie, locale, and identity input that changes the response.
Normalize tracking values and order-insensitive noise before lookup.
Test that two users or tenants cannot receive each other’s response.

variants.hint: Correctness before reuse, and isolation last as proof.
variants.explanation: Name → inputs → normalize → isolation test. Adding a value to the key fragments the cache; omitting one leaks or mis-serves responses.

variants.title: Design the cache key
variants.context: Two requests may share a cached response only when every input that can change the response is in the cache key or removed by safe normalization. Name the response, list its inputs, normalize noise, then test isolation.
variants.prompt: A localized landing page varies by language. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Use a versioned path for the page.
Record that the language input changes the body.
Normalize the language value to a small allowlist before the lookup.
Prove that private variants cannot cross between users.

variants.hint: The language belongs in the key only in its normalized form.
variants.explanation: Include only the normalized language dimension; raw Accept-Language values would fragment the cache into thousands of variants.

variants.title: Design the cache key
variants.context: Two requests may share a cached response only when every input that can change the response is in the cache key or removed by safe normalization. Name the response, list its inputs, normalize noise, then test isolation.
variants.prompt: An API response depends on a tenant header. Put the steps in order.

items.text: List the tenant header as a response input.
Strip campaign parameters that do not alter the response.
Test that tenant A can never receive tenant B’s cached body.

variants.hint: A tenant dimension is a correctness and security input.
variants.explanation: Tenant identity must be part of the key or the response must not be cached. Isolation testing proves the boundary.

variants.title: Decide what goes in the key
variants.context: Include a query string only when it selects the returned resource. Exclude tracking parameters. Forward a value without caching on it when the origin needs it but the response stays reusable. Never cache an authenticated response because its path looks public.
variants.prompt: URLs carry utm_source and utm_campaign parameters that never change the page. Should they be in the cache key?
options: No. Normalize them away so identical pages share one cached copy.
Yes. Every parameter must be in the key.
optionFeedback: Tracking parameters fragment the cache without changing the response.
Including noise multiplies origin traffic through needless variants.
Neither parameter changes the response.
variants.hint: Does the value change the response body?
variants.explanation: Exclude analytics and campaign parameters. Include a query string only when it chooses the returned representation.

variants.title: Decide what goes in the key
variants.context: Include a query string only when it selects the returned resource. Exclude tracking parameters. Forward a value without caching on it when the origin needs it but the response stays reusable. Never cache an authenticated response because its path looks public.
variants.prompt: An authenticated account page lives at /account, which looks like a public path. The default behavior caches it. What is wrong?
options: An authenticated response was cached because its path looked public; private content can be served to others.
optionFeedback: Never cache an authenticated response merely because the path appears public.
Path alone cannot tell CloudFront that a response is private.
TTL is irrelevant if the response must not be shared at all.
variants.hint: Which input changes this response that the key does not include?
variants.explanation: Private responses need identity in the key or must bypass the cache. Use signed URLs or cookies for private-content authorization.

variants.title: Decide what goes in the key
variants.context: Include a query string only when it selects the returned resource. Exclude tracking parameters. Forward a value without caching on it when the origin needs it but the response stays reusable. Never cache an authenticated response because its path looks public.
variants.prompt: The origin needs a device header for logging, but the response is identical for every device. Which policy?
options: Forward the header to the origin without including it in the cache key.
Add the header to the cache key.
optionFeedback: Forwarding without caching on it keeps reuse while giving the origin what it needs.
Keying on it fragments the cache for no correctness gain.
The origin needs the value for logging.
variants.hint: Separate what the origin needs from what changes the response.
variants.explanation: An origin request policy can forward a value that the cache policy leaves out of the key.

variants.title: Pick the edge boundary
variants.context: CloudFront Functions run lightweight JavaScript at viewer request or response. Lambda@Edge covers origin events and heavier logic. Database access, durable state, and business rules stay in an origin service.
variants.prompt: Tracking parameters must be stripped before the cache lookup on every request. Which boundary fits?
options: A CloudFront Function at viewer request.
optionFeedback: Lightweight normalization at viewer request runs before the cache lookup.
Origin-facing triggers run only on the origin path, after the cache decision.
The origin never sees a cache hit, so it cannot normalize the key.
variants.hint: Which phase runs before the cache lookup?
variants.explanation: Viewer-request functions shape the cache key; origin-facing triggers run only when CloudFront goes to the origin.

variants.title: Pick the edge boundary
variants.context: CloudFront Functions run lightweight JavaScript at viewer request or response. Lambda@Edge covers origin events and heavier logic. Database access, durable state, and business rules stay in an origin service.
variants.prompt: Logic needs an origin-response event and a supported library that CloudFront Functions cannot run. Which boundary?
optionFeedback: Lambda@Edge covers the four event phases and more execution resources.
CloudFront Functions handle viewer events only, with a small runtime.
Cache policies configure keys and TTLs, not code.
variants.hint: Which option has origin events and a fuller runtime?
variants.explanation: Use Lambda@Edge when logic needs an origin event, libraries, or capabilities outside the CloudFront Functions runtime.

variants.title: Pick the edge boundary
variants.context: CloudFront Functions run lightweight JavaScript at viewer request or response. Lambda@Edge covers origin events and heavier logic. Database access, durable state, and business rules stay in an origin service.
variants.prompt: A team wants Lambda@Edge to read the database and write orders. What is the better placement?
options: An origin service with explicit ownership and observability.
Lambda@Edge, since it runs closer to users.
optionFeedback: Durable state changes and business rules belong in a service you can own and observe.
Edge proximity does not make business authority a good fit at the edge.
CloudFront Functions cannot do this work and should not.
variants.explanation: Keep database access, durable state, and complex authorization in an origin service.

variants.title: Operate freshness and failure
variants.context: Use origin Cache-Control with a cache policy whose TTLs preserve the freshness promise. Version immutable assets instead of wildcard invalidations. A long error TTL can preserve an outage. Origin Shield consolidates simultaneous misses.
variants.prompt: After an origin outage is fixed, users keep seeing error pages for an hour. Why?
options: Error responses were cached with a long TTL, preserving the outage.
optionFeedback: Decide how errors are cached; a long error TTL outlives the incident.
The origin recovered; the cache did not.
DNS is unrelated to cached error bodies.
variants.hint: What did CloudFront store during the outage?
variants.explanation: Bound error caching so recovery is visible quickly, and separate content classes into behaviors.

variants.title: Operate freshness and failure
variants.context: Use origin Cache-Control with a cache policy whose TTLs preserve the freshness promise. Version immutable assets instead of wildcard invalidations. A long error TTL can preserve an outage. Origin Shield consolidates simultaneous misses.
variants.prompt: Every deployment runs a wildcard invalidation and origin load spikes. What is the better practice?
options: Version immutable assets so a changed asset gets a new name.
Set the maximum TTL to zero.
optionFeedback: Versioned names make deployments independent of invalidations.
More invalidations mean more cold misses.
Zero TTL removes the cache entirely.
variants.hint: How can a changed asset avoid sharing an old name?
variants.explanation: A changed immutable asset should receive a new name instead of relying on a broad invalidation.

variants.title: Operate freshness and failure
variants.context: Use origin Cache-Control with a cache policy whose TTLs preserve the freshness promise. Version immutable assets instead of wildcard invalidations. A long error TTL can preserve an outage. Origin Shield consolidates simultaneous misses.
variants.prompt: A popular video goes viral. Thousands of edges miss the same object at once. Which control reduces duplicate origin fetches?
options: Origin Shield, a centralized cache layer that consolidates simultaneous misses.
optionFeedback: Origin Shield sits in front of the origin and coalesces misses for the same object.
A shorter TTL creates more misses.
More edges mean more independent misses without a shared layer.
variants.hint: Where can duplicate misses be merged before the origin?
variants.explanation: Origin Shield adds a cache layer that reduces origin load when many edges miss the same object simultaneously.
